intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC5A1 gene (182380), which encodes the Na+/glucose cotransporter SGLT1, on chromosome 22q13.1.

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC5A1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Glucose-galactose malabsorption (GGM) is an autosomal recessive disease with life-threatening newborn diarrhea caused by mutations in the Na(+) /glucose cotransporter gene SLC5A1.
checks.explanation: The abstract says GGM is autosomal recessive and caused by SLC5A1 mutations. It also reports homozygous missense mutations that co-segregate with GGM in affected individuals.

checks.claim: The SLC5A1 gene encodes the Na+/glucose cotransporter SGLT1.
checks.evidence_quote: We have previously cloned and sequenced a Na+/glucose cotransporter from normal human ileum and shown that this gene, SGLT1, resides on the distal q arm of chromosome 22.
checks.explanation: SGLT1 is the gene for the Na+/glucose cotransporter. SLC5A1 is its approved gene symbol, so the draft's wording only restates standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: The SLC5A1 gene is located on chromosome 22q13.1.
checks.evidence_quote: caused by mutations in the Na(+) /glucose cotransporter gene SLC5A1
checks.explanation: The abstract does not state the chromosomal location. Under the fact-checking rules, a gene's chromosomal location counts as standard nomenclature and is accepted as restating the paper.

paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder that appears in the first weeks of life. It is defined by a selective failure of the intestine to absorb dietary glucose and galactose. The resulting severe diarrhea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991). The disorder is caused by a defect in SGLT1, the Na+/glucose cotransporter of the intestinal brush border (Martín et al., 1996).

checks.evidence_quote: Glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is an autosomal recessive disease

checks.evidence_quote: manifesting within the first weeks of life

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is defined by a selective failure of the intestine to absorb dietary glucose and galactose.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by a selective failure to absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption causes severe diarrhea and dehydration.
checks.evidence_quote: The consequent severe diarrhoea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are eliminated from the diet.

checks.claim: The severe diarrhea and dehydration of glucose/galactose malabsorption are usually fatal unless glucose and galactose are removed from the diet.
checks.evidence_quote: The consequent severe diarrhoea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are eliminated from the diet.

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is caused by a defect in SGLT1, the Na+/glucose cotransporter of the intestinal brush border.
checks.evidence_quote: the Na+/glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) couples sugar transport to Na+ gradients across the intestinal brush border. Glucose-Galactose Malabsorption (GGM) is caused by a defect in SGLT1.
checks.explanation: The abstract says GGM is caused by a defect in SGLT1 and describes SGLT1 as the Na+/glucose cotransporter of the intestinal brush border.

One child had a renal stone at the first visit, and another was found to have one on follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) found that normal human jejunal mucosa transported glucose against a concentration gradient. This transport was saturable, depended on sodium and energy, and showed competitive inhibition. Mucosa from 6 normal controls and from the proband's asymptomatic 5-year-old brother concentrated glucose to 16 times the medium concentration. All subjects accumulated fructose in a similar way. Intestinal glucose transport was impaired in both parents and in a half sister of the proband, with values falling between those of normal controls and the proband. In these heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired but efflux was the same as in controls. Kinetic analysis showed reduced capacity (Vmax) with normal affinity (Km). The authors concluded that heterozygotes can be detected.

paragraphs.text: Martín et al. (1996) performed prenatal screening for GGM in 2 later pregnancies within a large consanguineous family. paragraphs.text: Xin and Wang (2011) studied 33 patients with GGM from a large Old Order Amish pedigree.
